--- title: The Python Standard Library --- ## Goals 1. Understand what a Python package is and how to `import` it in a script or interactive environment. 2. Become familiar with a few Python packages relevant to data analysis. 3. Learn about the help system in Python, which is useful in learning about functions and objects defined by packages. ## What is the Python standard library? By now we have encountered various symbols in the Python language representing language constructs, built-in functions, and type constructors. In principle, you could use these tools to build up *almost* any tools you might need; for example, you could write a tool to read a spreadsheet file and represent its data within Python. Fortunately, many important functions for analytics have already been written by experts and are available as *modules It behooves any programmer to become familiar with *the standard library* of any language, which is a collection of code modules that are part of the language but kept separate for several reasons. - **Keeping an uncluttered namespace by default**. + When you start up an interactive Python session, you have access to various functions and object types by default. + Separating some functionality into modules lets a user opt-in to features they would like to use. + This helps keep names as simple as possible. - **Ease of maintenance**. + Several developers work on the core Python language. + Keeping some features, like the `math` module, separate from the core language allows people to work on the core language without blocking improvements and bug fixes in the `math` module, and *vice versa*. - **Code organization**. + The details of how to compute `sin(x)` within the `math` module has little to do with how a computer reads a comma-separated values (CSV) file. + Grouping related concepts under a particular module creates a **namespace**, a universe of related symbols. + Namespaces make it easier for people to discover and use functions. ### What is a Python module? A **Python module** is a *file* of Python code written to implement a set of related functions and objects. - Can be (but not always) implemented as a simple `.py` file. - Defines a namespace so that function names are relatively simple, at least within a module. - Can use functionality from other modules. - We will write our own Python modules in the future. ### What is a Python package? A **Python package** is a collection of related *Python modules*. - Can be a single directory containing modules, or a directory with subdirectories. - Again, the purpose is to organize related concepts, functions, and objects while controlling namespaces. - There is an additional structure to packages that we will discuss at a later date. ### How do we use them? Conceptually, a Python *module* and a Python *package* are nearly identical and this is essentially the case from a user perspective. Any time we want to use one of these tools, we must **import** the module/package. The syntax for using functions and objects from an imported module/package will depend on *how* we import it. The following examples illustrate the most common ways programmers import code from modules/packages. #### Example 1: `import` The following makes the `math` module available in the current scope. ::: {#a2572d2a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import math ``` ::: Now we can reference functions and objects by prepending `math.` to calls and references. ::: {#eb0d168a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} math.sqrt(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1.4142135623730951 ``` ::: ::: If you do this with a *package*, you only import functions and object types defined directly within the named package. For performance reasons, you must specifically import any submodules you wish to use. The following code fails because `request` is a submodule of `urllib`, which is not imported below. ::: {#4bce8546 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import urllib urllib.request.urlopen("https://example.com") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AttributeError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[3], line 3
      1 import urllib
      2 
----> 3 urllib.request.urlopen("https://example.com")

AttributeError: module 'urllib' has no attribute 'request'
``` ::: ::: ::: #### Example 2: `from import ` If you want to import specific functions or object types, use the `from X import Y, Z` syntax. This lets you use imports without qualification. ::: {#0bf43337 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from statistics import mean, median mydata = [100, 92, 79, 85] print(f"The mean is {mean(mydata)} and the median is {median(mydata)}.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` The mean is 89 and the median is 88.5. ``` ::: ::: #### Example 3: `import ... as ...` Use this import style to *alias* a module name to a shorter one. Many Python modules/packages have canonical aliases. The following is a common shorthand for the Pandas package, which we will learn about later in the course. It has already been installed for you when you set up the class Docker container. ::: {#ec02719d .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd pd.DataFrame({'name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carlos'], 'age': [28, 29, 35]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
name age
0 Alice 28
1 Bob 29
2 Carlos 35
``` ::: ::: #### Example 4: `from import ` Similar to Example 2 above, this lets you import submodules without qualification. ::: {#6d15f196 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from urllib import request request.urlopen("https://example.com") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` ``` ::: ::: ## Numerical computation ### `math` Various math-related functions. ::: {#f8ad4a2f .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # A = P * e^(r*t), continuously compunded interest formula def future_value_cts(principal, rate, time): return principal * math.exp(rate * time) future_value_cts(100.0, 0.05, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 110.51709180756477 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#ac180f4b .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} def circle_area(radius): return math.pi * radius**2 circle_area(1.) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` 3.141592653589793 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#95b5f285 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} math.log(math.exp(1)) # natural logarithm ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` 1.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#a848a971 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} math.log10(10.0) # base 10 logarithm ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` 1.0 ``` ::: ::: ### `statistics` Implements various concepts in statistics. We will use this package sparingly as there is a much richer functionality implemented in other Python packages. ::: {#ab3857e4 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} from statistics import mean, median, variance, stdev, quantiles salaries = [100000, 110000, 80000, 320000] ``` ::: ::: {#52f96a1e .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} mean(salaries) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` 152500 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#bd07c1b6 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} variance(salaries) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` 12625000000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#baa0b72a .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} stdev(salaries) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` 112361.02527122117 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#a4ba6fe1 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} quantiles(salaries, n = 2) # returns median ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` [105000.0] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#dc0fe0b1 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} quantiles(salaries, n = 4) # returns quartiles, Q1, Q2 (median), Q3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` [85000.0, 105000.0, 267500.0] ``` ::: ::: ### `random` Used to sample from "brand name" distributions or collections in Python. We will later defer to `numpy.random` once we discuss the Numpy package. ::: {#d0741fac .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} import random # Normal distribution with mean 10 and standard deviation 1 random.normalvariate(mu = 10.0, sigma = 1.0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` 10.506384366273174 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#3a26c4f3 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} # make it reproducible with a seed random.seed(1234) x = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carlos"] print(random.choice(x)) print(random.choice(x)) print(random.choice(x)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bob Alice Alice ``` ::: :::
